title: What Is Python & Why Learn It?
script:
Python is a high-level, readable programming language used for automation, web development, data, AI, scripting, and more. [Visual: clean programming course title card, What Is Python & Why Learn It?, modern code editor]
In this course we will start from zero: writing code, storing data, making decisions, repeating tasks, organizing data, building functions, handling files and errors, learning object-oriented programming, and finally building projects. [Visual: animated programming concept, What Is Python & Why Learn It?, clean educational graphics]
You do not need previous programming experience. [Visual: animated programming concept, What Is Python & Why Learn It?, clean educational graphics]
The goal is not to memorize syntax. [Visual: animated programming concept, What Is Python & Why Learn It?, clean educational graphics]
The goal is to understand what each piece of code does and practice it. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating What Is Python & Why Learn It?]
Challenge: Name three things Python can be used for. Answer: automation, AI/data, and web development are three examples. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Install Python + VS Code
script:
Before writing real programs, we need a working environment. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Install Python + VS Code, modern code editor]
Install a current Python 3 release from the official Python website, then install VS Code. [Visual: animated programming concept, Install Python + VS Code, clean educational graphics]
In VS Code, install the Python extension. [Visual: animated programming concept, Install Python + VS Code, clean educational graphics]
Open a terminal and run python --version, or py --version on Windows. [Visual: animated programming concept, Install Python + VS Code, clean educational graphics]
If you see a Python 3 version, the interpreter is ready. [Visual: animated programming concept, Install Python + VS Code, clean educational graphics]
Create a file named main.py. [Visual: animated programming concept, Install Python + VS Code, clean educational graphics]
We will use this file throughout the course. [Visual: animated programming concept, Install Python + VS Code, clean educational graphics]
If Windows opens the Microsoft Store instead, check that Python was installed correctly and that the Python launcher is available. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Install Python + VS Code]
Challenge: Create main.py and make sure Python reports a version. Answer: run python --version or py --version. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Your First Python Program
script:
A Python program is simply instructions that Python executes. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Your First Python Program, modern code editor]
Create main.py and write one print statement. [Visual: animated programming concept, Your First Python Program, clean educational graphics]
Then run the file from VS Code. [Visual: animated programming concept, Your First Python Program, clean educational graphics]
Notice that Python executes the statement and displays the result. [Visual: animated programming concept, Your First Python Program, clean educational graphics]
The important idea is the flow: we write source code, Python interprets or executes it, and we see an output. [Visual: animated programming concept, Your First Python Program, clean educational graphics]
From now on, every new concept will follow this pattern: understand it, see a small example, then change the code yourself. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Your First Python Program]
Challenge: Print your name and the words 'I am learning Python'. Answer: use two print statements with strings. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: print()
script:
The print function sends information to the console. [Visual: clean programming course title card, print(), modern code editor]
Text goes inside quotes, while numbers can be written directly. [Visual: animated programming concept, print(), clean educational graphics]
You can print several values by separating them with commas. [Visual: animated programming concept, print(), clean educational graphics]
Python automatically puts spaces between comma-separated values. [Visual: animated programming concept, print(), clean educational graphics]
You can also control the ending with the end argument, although we will keep that simple for now. [Visual: animated programming concept, print(), clean educational graphics]
Remember: print displays a value; it does not permanently store it. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating print()]
Challenge: Print your name, age, and favorite language on separate lines. Answer: use three print calls. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Comments
script:
Comments are notes for humans. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Comments, modern code editor]
Python ignores text after a hash symbol on a line. [Visual: animated programming concept, Comments, clean educational graphics]
Comments are useful for explaining why code exists, marking sections, and temporarily disabling a line while testing. [Visual: animated programming concept, Comments, clean educational graphics]
Do not turn every line into a comment; clear code should explain itself when possible. [Visual: animated programming concept, Comments, clean educational graphics]
We will use short comments throughout the course to make examples easier to follow. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Comments]
Challenge: Add a comment above a print statement explaining what it does. Answer: start the note with #. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Variables
script:
A variable is a name that refers to a value. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Variables, modern code editor]
Think of it as a labeled box. [Visual: animated programming concept, Variables, clean educational graphics]
You create one with a name, an equals sign, and a value. [Visual: animated programming concept, Variables, clean educational graphics]
Python figures out the value's type automatically. [Visual: animated programming concept, Variables, clean educational graphics]
Variables can be changed later, and the new value replaces the old one. [Visual: animated programming concept, Variables, clean educational graphics]
Use clear names such as age, username, or score. [Visual: animated programming concept, Variables, clean educational graphics]
Avoid confusing names and remember that Python is case-sensitive: age and Age are different names. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Variables]
Challenge: Create variables for a name, age, and favorite game, then print them. Answer: assign each value with = and print the variables. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Data Types
script:
Python values have types. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Data Types, modern code editor]
A string, or str, represents text. [Visual: animated programming concept, Data Types, clean educational graphics]
An int is a whole number. [Visual: animated programming concept, Data Types, clean educational graphics]
A float is a decimal number. [Visual: animated programming concept, Data Types, clean educational graphics]
A bool is either True or False. [Visual: animated programming concept, Data Types, clean educational graphics]
Knowing the type matters because operations depend on it. [Visual: animated programming concept, Data Types, clean educational graphics]
For example, adding two integers performs arithmetic, while adding two strings joins text. [Visual: animated programming concept, Data Types, clean educational graphics]
You can inspect a value with type(). [Visual: animated programming concept, Data Types, clean educational graphics]
Python is dynamically typed, so a variable can later refer to a different type, although changing types carelessly can cause bugs. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Data Types]
Challenge: Create one value of each of the four basic types. Answer: use text, whole number, decimal, and True/False. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Numbers & Math
script:
Python can work like a calculator. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Numbers & Math, modern code editor]
The main operators are plus, minus, multiplication, division, floor division, remainder, and exponentiation. [Visual: animated programming concept, Numbers & Math, clean educational graphics]
Regular division with slash returns a decimal. [Visual: animated programming concept, Numbers & Math, clean educational graphics]
Floor division uses double slash. [Visual: animated programming concept, Numbers & Math, clean educational graphics]
The percent operator gives the remainder, which is useful for checking whether a number is even or for repeating cycles. [Visual: animated programming concept, Numbers & Math, clean educational graphics]
Python follows normal mathematical precedence, so multiplication happens before addition unless parentheses change the order. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Numbers & Math]
Challenge: Find the remainder when 17 is divided by 5. Answer: 17 % 5 gives 2. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Strings
script:
Strings are sequences of characters. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Strings, modern code editor]
You can use single or double quotes to create them. [Visual: animated programming concept, Strings, clean educational graphics]
The plus operator can join strings, but when you need to mix variables with text, f-strings are usually cleaner. [Visual: animated programming concept, Strings, clean educational graphics]
Strings also support indexing, starting at zero, and slicing. [Visual: animated programming concept, Strings, clean educational graphics]
We will explore methods in the next lesson. [Visual: animated programming concept, Strings, clean educational graphics]
For now, focus on treating text as data that your program can store and manipulate. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Strings]
Challenge: Print the first three characters of a word using slicing. Answer: word[0:3]. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: String Methods
script:
String methods are built-in tools attached to string values. [Visual: clean programming course title card, String Methods, modern code editor]
lower and upper change letter case. [Visual: animated programming concept, String Methods, clean educational graphics]
strip removes surrounding whitespace. [Visual: animated programming concept, String Methods, clean educational graphics]
replace swaps text. [Visual: animated programming concept, String Methods, clean educational graphics]
split turns a string into a list. [Visual: animated programming concept, String Methods, clean educational graphics]
startswith and endswith test prefixes and suffixes. [Visual: animated programming concept, String Methods, clean educational graphics]
Methods usually return a new value rather than changing the original string. [Visual: animated programming concept, String Methods, clean educational graphics]
This becomes important when processing user input or data from files. [Visual: animated programming concept, String Methods, clean educational graphics]
Learn the idea of calling a method with a dot; you can look up specific methods when you need them. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating String Methods]
Challenge: Turn '  PYTHON  ' into 'python'. Answer: text.strip().lower(). [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: User Input
script:
The input function pauses your program and waits for the user to type something. [Visual: clean programming course title card, User Input, modern code editor]
The result of input is always a string, even if the user types a number. [Visual: animated programming concept, User Input, clean educational graphics]
You can store it in a variable and use it later. [Visual: animated programming concept, User Input, clean educational graphics]
This is the first step toward interactive programs. [Visual: animated programming concept, User Input, clean educational graphics]
Combine input with f-strings to create useful messages. [Visual: animated programming concept, User Input, clean educational graphics]
In the next lesson, we will convert numeric input so Python can calculate with it. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating User Input]
Challenge: Ask for a favorite game and print a sentence containing it. Answer: store input in a variable and use an f-string. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Type Conversion
script:
Because input returns strings, numeric calculations require conversion. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Type Conversion, modern code editor]
int converts to a whole number, float converts to a decimal, str converts to text, and bool converts to a Boolean with rules you should understand. [Visual: animated programming concept, Type Conversion, clean educational graphics]
Conversion can fail if the text is not a valid number, so later we will learn error handling. [Visual: animated programming concept, Type Conversion, clean educational graphics]
Use conversion exactly where you need it rather than converting everything automatically. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Type Conversion]
Challenge: Ask for two numbers and print their sum. Answer: convert both inputs with int or float before adding. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Comparison Operators
script:
Comparison operators produce Boolean values. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Comparison Operators, modern code editor]
Double equals checks equality; a single equals assigns a value. [Visual: animated programming concept, Comparison Operators, clean educational graphics]
Not equal is written !=. [Visual: animated programming concept, Comparison Operators, clean educational graphics]
Greater than and less than compare numeric values, while greater-or-equal and less-or-equal include equality. [Visual: animated programming concept, Comparison Operators, clean educational graphics]
Comparisons become especially useful inside if statements. [Visual: animated programming concept, Comparison Operators, clean educational graphics]
You can compare strings too, but for beginners focus first on numbers and exact text comparisons. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Comparison Operators]
Challenge: Check whether score is at least 50. Answer: score >= 50. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Logical Operators
script:
Logical operators let you build larger conditions. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Logical Operators, modern code editor]
and requires both conditions to be true. [Visual: animated programming concept, Logical Operators, clean educational graphics]
or requires at least one to be true. [Visual: animated programming concept, Logical Operators, clean educational graphics]
not reverses a Boolean result. [Visual: animated programming concept, Logical Operators, clean educational graphics]
Imagine checking access: a person may need a valid password and an active account. [Visual: animated programming concept, Logical Operators, clean educational graphics]
Or imagine accepting either of two valid choices. [Visual: animated programming concept, Logical Operators, clean educational graphics]
Parentheses can make complex expressions easier to read. [Visual: animated programming concept, Logical Operators, clean educational graphics]
Understanding these operators will make your decision-making code much more powerful. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Logical Operators]
Challenge: Write a condition that is true only when score is at least 50 and attendance is True. Answer: score >= 50 and attendance. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: if Statements
script:
An if statement gives your program a decision. [Visual: clean programming course title card, if Statements, modern code editor]
Python evaluates the condition, and if it is True, the indented block runs. [Visual: animated programming concept, if Statements, clean educational graphics]
Indentation is part of Python syntax, so keep the block consistently indented. [Visual: animated programming concept, if Statements, clean educational graphics]
Start with simple decisions before combining many conditions. [Visual: animated programming concept, if Statements, clean educational graphics]
The pattern is if, condition, colon, then an indented block. [Visual: animated programming concept, if Statements, clean educational graphics]
This is one of the most important structures in programming because it lets software react to data. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating if Statements]
Challenge: Print 'Pass' when score is at least 50. Answer: if score >= 50: then print('Pass'). [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: elif and else
script:
Use else when you need a fallback and elif when there are additional conditions. [Visual: clean programming course title card, elif and else, modern code editor]
Python checks the branches from top to bottom and executes the first matching branch. [Visual: animated programming concept, elif and else, clean educational graphics]
That means order matters. [Visual: animated programming concept, elif and else, clean educational graphics]
Put more specific conditions before broader ones. [Visual: animated programming concept, elif and else, clean educational graphics]
Only one branch in an if/elif/else chain runs. [Visual: animated programming concept, elif and else, clean educational graphics]
This makes the structure useful for grades, menus, categories, and many other choices. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating elif and else]
Challenge: Create three score categories: 90+ excellent, 50+ pass, otherwise fail. Answer: use if, elif, else in that order. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Nested Conditions
script:
A nested condition is an if statement inside another if statement. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Nested Conditions, modern code editor]
It is useful when the second decision only matters after the first decision succeeds. [Visual: animated programming concept, Nested Conditions, clean educational graphics]
For example, check whether someone is logged in, then check whether they are an admin. [Visual: animated programming concept, Nested Conditions, clean educational graphics]
Do not overuse nesting; if conditions become deeply nested, combining conditions or using functions can make the code clearer. [Visual: animated programming concept, Nested Conditions, clean educational graphics]
The key concept is that indentation shows which decision owns each block. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Nested Conditions]
Challenge: Print 'Premium content' only when logged_in and premium are both true. Answer: nest or combine the conditions. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Conditional Practice
script:
Let's turn decisions into a small program. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Conditional Practice, modern code editor]
We will ask for a temperature and classify it. [Visual: animated programming concept, Conditional Practice, clean educational graphics]
The important part is not the exact categories; it is learning to translate a rule into code. [Visual: animated programming concept, Conditional Practice, clean educational graphics]
First get input, convert it to a number, then test conditions from highest priority to lowest. [Visual: animated programming concept, Conditional Practice, clean educational graphics]
When a program gives the wrong category, check the condition order and boundaries carefully. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Conditional Practice]
Challenge: Add a fourth category for 10 or below called 'Cold'. Answer: place elif temp > 10 before else, or make the final else cover 10 and below. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: for Loops
script:
A for loop repeats a block once for each item in a sequence. [Visual: clean programming course title card, for Loops, modern code editor]
The variable after for receives the current item. [Visual: animated programming concept, for Loops, clean educational graphics]
This is cleaner than manually writing the same statement many times. [Visual: animated programming concept, for Loops, clean educational graphics]
Start with a list of names or a string. [Visual: animated programming concept, for Loops, clean educational graphics]
Python takes care of moving to the next item. [Visual: animated programming concept, for Loops, clean educational graphics]
Later, range will let us repeat code a specific number of times. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating for Loops]
Challenge: Loop over the string 'Python' and print each character. Answer: for char in 'Python': print(char). [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: range()
script:
range is commonly used when you need a sequence of numbers. [Visual: clean programming course title card, range(), modern code editor]
range(5) produces 0 through 4. [Visual: animated programming concept, range(), clean educational graphics]
You can give a start and stop, and optionally a step. [Visual: animated programming concept, range(), clean educational graphics]
The stop value is not included. [Visual: animated programming concept, range(), clean educational graphics]
This is called a half-open range and is extremely common in programming. [Visual: animated programming concept, range(), clean educational graphics]
Remember: range does not normally create a visible list; it produces a range object that a loop can iterate over. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating range()]
Challenge: Print numbers 1 through 10. Answer: for i in range(1, 11): print(i). [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: while Loops
script:
A while loop keeps running as long as its condition is True. [Visual: clean programming course title card, while Loops, modern code editor]
This is useful when you do not know in advance how many repetitions you need. [Visual: animated programming concept, while Loops, clean educational graphics]
You must make sure something changes so the condition eventually becomes false, unless an intentional infinite loop is the goal. [Visual: animated programming concept, while Loops, clean educational graphics]
A counter is a simple example. [Visual: animated programming concept, while Loops, clean educational graphics]
Later, break can provide another way to stop a loop. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating while Loops]
Challenge: Create a countdown from 5 to 1. Answer: start count at 5, print it, then subtract one each loop. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: break
script:
break immediately exits the nearest loop. [Visual: clean programming course title card, break, modern code editor]
It is useful when you have found what you are looking for or when a user chooses to quit. [Visual: animated programming concept, break, clean educational graphics]
Think of it as an emergency exit for the current loop. [Visual: animated programming concept, break, clean educational graphics]
The loop after the break does not continue. [Visual: animated programming concept, break, clean educational graphics]
Use it intentionally and keep the condition that triggers it clear so readers can understand why the loop stops. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating break]
Challenge: Loop through numbers 1 to 10 and stop when the number is 6. Answer: use if number == 6: break. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: continue
script:
continue skips the rest of the current loop iteration and moves to the next iteration. [Visual: clean programming course title card, continue, modern code editor]
Unlike break, it does not stop the loop. [Visual: animated programming concept, continue, clean educational graphics]
It is useful for filtering unwanted values. [Visual: animated programming concept, continue, clean educational graphics]
For example, you can skip even numbers and process only odd numbers. [Visual: animated programming concept, continue, clean educational graphics]
Keep the skipped condition obvious, because too many continue statements can make a loop harder to follow. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating continue]
Challenge: Print only numbers from 1 to 10 that are not divisible by 3. Answer: if number % 3 == 0: continue. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Nested Loops
script:
A nested loop runs the inner loop for every iteration of the outer loop. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Nested Loops, modern code editor]
This is useful for grids, tables, combinations, and simple patterns. [Visual: animated programming concept, Nested Loops, clean educational graphics]
If the outer loop runs three times and the inner loop runs four times, the inner block can run twelve times. [Visual: animated programming concept, Nested Loops, clean educational graphics]
Nested loops can become expensive with large data, so use them carefully. [Visual: animated programming concept, Nested Loops, clean educational graphics]
For now, focus on understanding which variable belongs to which loop. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Nested Loops]
Challenge: Print a 3 by 3 coordinate grid. Answer: use two range(3) loops and print row and col. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Loop Challenges
script:
Now we combine loop skills. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Loop Challenges, modern code editor]
A common pattern is an accumulator: start total at zero, then add each value. [Visual: animated programming concept, Loop Challenges, clean educational graphics]
Another pattern is a counter: start at zero and increase it when a condition matches. [Visual: animated programming concept, Loop Challenges, clean educational graphics]
These patterns appear everywhere in real programs. [Visual: animated programming concept, Loop Challenges, clean educational graphics]
Read the code line by line and ask what the variable means before and after each iteration. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Loop Challenges]
Challenge: Find the total of [3, 5, 8]. Answer: initialize total = 0 and add each n. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Common Loop Mistakes
script:
Three beginner loop mistakes are especially common. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Common Loop Mistakes, modern code editor]
First, a while loop may never change its condition and become infinite. [Visual: animated programming concept, Common Loop Mistakes, clean educational graphics]
Second, range stops before its end value, so range(1, 5) gives 1 through 4. [Visual: animated programming concept, Common Loop Mistakes, clean educational graphics]
Third, indentation can put a statement outside the loop by accident. [Visual: animated programming concept, Common Loop Mistakes, clean educational graphics]
When debugging, print the loop variable and ask whether it changes as expected. [Visual: animated programming concept, Common Loop Mistakes, clean educational graphics]
Small diagnostic prints are often faster than guessing. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Common Loop Mistakes]
Challenge: Why is while count < 3: with no count change dangerous? Answer: the condition stays true forever. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Practical Loop Project
script:
Let's build a tiny practical program. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Practical Loop Project, modern code editor]
The user gets a limited number of attempts to enter a password. [Visual: animated programming concept, Practical Loop Project, clean educational graphics]
We will use a for loop, input, comparison, and break. [Visual: animated programming concept, Practical Loop Project, clean educational graphics]
This demonstrates how loops and decisions work together. [Visual: animated programming concept, Practical Loop Project, clean educational graphics]
Real authentication systems need much more security; this is only a learning example. [Visual: animated programming concept, Practical Loop Project, clean educational graphics]
The goal is to understand control flow, not to build production security. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Practical Loop Project]
Challenge: Add a message when all attempts are used. Answer: use an else block on the for loop or track success. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Revision: Decisions & Loops
script:
You should now be able to make programs choose and repeat. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Revision: Decisions & Loops, modern code editor]
Review if, elif, else; comparison and logical operators; for and while; range; break; continue; and nested loops. [Visual: animated programming concept, Revision: Decisions & Loops, clean educational graphics]
The key skill is translating a rule into control flow. [Visual: animated programming concept, Revision: Decisions & Loops, clean educational graphics]
If a problem says 'repeat for each item,' think for. [Visual: animated programming concept, Revision: Decisions & Loops, clean educational graphics]
If it says 'keep going until something happens,' think while. [Visual: animated programming concept, Revision: Decisions & Loops, clean educational graphics]
If it says 'choose based on a condition,' think if. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Revision: Decisions & Loops]
Challenge: Explain what the code prints. Answer: 1, 2, 4, 5. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

script:
This exam checks whether you can choose the correct control structure. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Exam #2: Decisions & Loops, modern code editor]
Try the questions without looking at the answer. [Visual: animated programming concept, Exam #2: Decisions & Loops, clean educational graphics]

title: Lists
script:
A list stores multiple values in one ordered collection. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Lists, modern code editor]
Lists can contain numbers, strings, or even other collections. [Visual: animated programming concept, Lists, clean educational graphics]
Indexing starts at zero, so the first item is index 0. [Visual: animated programming concept, Lists, clean educational graphics]
Lists are mutable, meaning you can change their contents. [Visual: animated programming concept, Lists, clean educational graphics]
Use square brackets to create them. [Visual: animated programming concept, Lists, clean educational graphics]
Lists are one of the most important Python data structures because they make it easy to work with groups of related values. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Lists]
Challenge: Create a list of three games and print the second one. Answer: games[1]. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: List Indexing
script:
List indexing lets you access a specific position. [Visual: clean programming course title card, List Indexing, modern code editor]
Positive indexes start at zero from the left. [Visual: animated programming concept, List Indexing, clean educational graphics]
Negative indexes start at -1 from the right, so -1 means the last item. [Visual: animated programming concept, List Indexing, clean educational graphics]
An index outside the list causes an IndexError. [Visual: animated programming concept, List Indexing, clean educational graphics]
When you are unsure how long a list is, use len. [Visual: animated programming concept, List Indexing, clean educational graphics]
Indexing is the foundation for slicing and many list algorithms. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating List Indexing]
Challenge: Get the last item without knowing the list length. Answer: items[-1]. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: List Slicing
script:
Slicing uses start:stop:step. [Visual: clean programming course title card, List Slicing, modern code editor]
The start is included, the stop is excluded, and the step controls movement. [Visual: animated programming concept, List Slicing, clean educational graphics]
You can omit values to slice from the beginning or to the end. [Visual: animated programming concept, List Slicing, clean educational graphics]
Slicing does not normally modify the original list; it creates a new list. [Visual: animated programming concept, List Slicing, clean educational graphics]
The same basic slicing idea also works with strings and other sequence types. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating List Slicing]
Challenge: Get [2, 3, 4] from nums. Answer: nums[2:5]. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: List Methods
script:
List methods let you change and manage collections. [Visual: clean programming course title card, List Methods, modern code editor]
append adds one item to the end. [Visual: animated programming concept, List Methods, clean educational graphics]
extend adds multiple items. [Visual: animated programming concept, List Methods, clean educational graphics]
insert places an item at a position. [Visual: animated programming concept, List Methods, clean educational graphics]
remove deletes the first matching value. [Visual: animated programming concept, List Methods, clean educational graphics]
pop removes and returns an item, commonly the last item. [Visual: animated programming concept, List Methods, clean educational graphics]
sort orders a list in place. [Visual: animated programming concept, List Methods, clean educational graphics]
Learn what each method returns as well as what it changes; for example, sort returns None because it modifies the list. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating List Methods]
Challenge: Add 10 to the end of a list. Answer: list.append(10). [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Looping Lists
script:
Lists become powerful when combined with loops. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Looping Lists, modern code editor]
A for loop can visit every item without needing indexes. [Visual: animated programming concept, Looping Lists, clean educational graphics]
If you need the position too, enumerate is a clean option that we will study later. [Visual: animated programming concept, Looping Lists, clean educational graphics]
You can also build totals, find values, or apply conditions while looping. [Visual: animated programming concept, Looping Lists, clean educational graphics]
Start by printing each item, then change the loop body to perform a useful task. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Looping Lists]
Challenge: Print only scores that are at least 70. Answer: add if score >= 70 inside the loop. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: List Challenges
script:
Let's practice finding a maximum, counting matches, and building a filtered list. [Visual: clean programming course title card, List Challenges, modern code editor]
Python has built-in functions for many of these jobs, but writing the loop yourself teaches the underlying logic. [Visual: animated programming concept, List Challenges, clean educational graphics]
When solving a problem, define the output first, then decide what information you need to track. [Visual: animated programming concept, List Challenges, clean educational graphics]
A variable like highest, count, or result usually represents the state of your algorithm. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating List Challenges]
Challenge: Count values greater than 5. Answer: start count=0 and increment when n > 5. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Tuples
script:
A tuple looks like a list but uses parentheses and is immutable. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Tuples, modern code editor]
Once created, you cannot replace or remove its items. [Visual: animated programming concept, Tuples, clean educational graphics]
Tuples are useful for fixed groups of values such as coordinates, RGB values, or records that should not be changed accidentally. [Visual: animated programming concept, Tuples, clean educational graphics]
You can still index and slice tuples and loop over them. [Visual: animated programming concept, Tuples, clean educational graphics]
Immutability can make intent clearer. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Tuples]
Challenge: Create a tuple containing a username and age. Answer: user = ('John', 17). [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Sets
script:
A set is an unordered collection of unique values. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Sets, modern code editor]
If you add a duplicate, the set keeps only one copy. [Visual: animated programming concept, Sets, clean educational graphics]
Sets are useful for removing duplicates and checking membership. [Visual: animated programming concept, Sets, clean educational graphics]
You can add and remove items, and you can calculate unions and intersections. [Visual: animated programming concept, Sets, clean educational graphics]
Because sets are unordered, do not rely on a particular display order. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Sets]
Challenge: Remove duplicates from [1,1,2,2,3]. Answer: set([1,1,2,2,3]) gives {1,2,3}. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Dictionaries
script:
A dictionary maps keys to values. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Dictionaries, modern code editor]
Think of it like a labeled record: username maps to a name, age maps to an age, and so on. [Visual: animated programming concept, Dictionaries, clean educational graphics]
Create dictionaries with curly braces and key:value pairs. [Visual: animated programming concept, Dictionaries, clean educational graphics]
Keys should be hashable, and common keys are strings or numbers. [Visual: animated programming concept, Dictionaries, clean educational graphics]
Dictionaries are central to Python because many APIs, JSON documents, and configuration objects use this structure. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Dictionaries]
Challenge: Add a score key with value 100. Answer: user['score'] = 100. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Dictionary Methods
script:
Dictionary methods make access safer and iteration easier. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Dictionary Methods, modern code editor]
get can return a default instead of raising a KeyError when a key is missing. [Visual: animated programming concept, Dictionary Methods, clean educational graphics]
keys returns keys, values returns values, and items returns key-value pairs. [Visual: animated programming concept, Dictionary Methods, clean educational graphics]
update merges or replaces entries. [Visual: animated programming concept, Dictionary Methods, clean educational graphics]
pop removes a key and returns its value. [Visual: animated programming concept, Dictionary Methods, clean educational graphics]
These methods are common when working with structured data. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Dictionary Methods]
Challenge: Safely read a missing 'score' key with default 0. Answer: user.get('score', 0). [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Looping Dictionaries
script:
Dictionaries can be looped in several ways. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Looping Dictionaries, modern code editor]
A plain for loop gives keys. [Visual: animated programming concept, Looping Dictionaries, clean educational graphics]
Use values when you only need values, and items when you need both the key and value. [Visual: animated programming concept, Looping Dictionaries, clean educational graphics]
This makes dictionary processing concise and readable. [Visual: animated programming concept, Looping Dictionaries, clean educational graphics]
A common pattern is to build a report by printing each key and value or to count categories. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Looping Dictionaries]
Challenge: Print only names with scores above 90. Answer: loop over items and check score > 90. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Nested Data
script:
Real data is often nested. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Nested Data, modern code editor]
A list may contain dictionaries, or a dictionary may contain lists. [Visual: animated programming concept, Nested Data, clean educational graphics]
Accessing nested data means following the structure one level at a time. [Visual: animated programming concept, Nested Data, clean educational graphics]
For example, users[0]['name'] gets the name from the first user dictionary. [Visual: animated programming concept, Nested Data, clean educational graphics]
Before writing complex expressions, inspect the data shape. [Visual: animated programming concept, Nested Data, clean educational graphics]
This habit prevents many indexing mistakes. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Nested Data]
Challenge: Print Mona's age. Answer: users[1]['age']. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Strings + Collections
script:
A common task is turning text into structured data. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Strings + Collections, modern code editor]
split can turn a comma-separated string into a list. [Visual: animated programming concept, Strings + Collections, clean educational graphics]
strip can clean spaces, and join can combine a list back into one string. [Visual: animated programming concept, Strings + Collections, clean educational graphics]
This pattern appears in logs, simple configuration files, user input, and data processing. [Visual: animated programming concept, Strings + Collections, clean educational graphics]
Always consider whether whitespace should be cleaned before comparison. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Strings + Collections]
Challenge: Split 'red blue green' into words. Answer: text.split(). [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: List Comprehensions
script:
A list comprehension is a compact way to build a list. [Visual: clean programming course title card, List Comprehensions, modern code editor]
The basic pattern is [expression for item in iterable]. [Visual: animated programming concept, List Comprehensions, clean educational graphics]
You can add an if condition to filter items. [Visual: animated programming concept, List Comprehensions, clean educational graphics]
They are useful when the transformation is simple and readable. [Visual: animated programming concept, List Comprehensions, clean educational graphics]
If a comprehension becomes complicated, a normal loop may be clearer. [Visual: animated programming concept, List Comprehensions, clean educational graphics]
Learn the long version first, then recognize the shorter form. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating List Comprehensions]
Challenge: Create doubled values from [1,2,3]. Answer: [n * 2 for n in [1,2,3]]. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Dictionary Comprehensions
script:
Dictionary comprehensions use a similar idea but produce key-value pairs: {key: value for item in iterable}. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Dictionary Comprehensions, modern code editor]
They are useful for transformations such as mapping numbers to their squares or filtering entries. [Visual: animated programming concept, Dictionary Comprehensions, clean educational graphics]
Keep the expression simple. [Visual: animated programming concept, Dictionary Comprehensions, clean educational graphics]
If you need multiple steps or complicated conditions, a regular loop may be easier to maintain. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Dictionary Comprehensions]
Challenge: Create a dictionary mapping each word to its length. Answer: {word: len(word) for word in words}. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Choosing Data Structures
script:
The right data structure depends on what the data means. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Choosing Data Structures, modern code editor]
Use a list for an ordered, changeable sequence. [Visual: animated programming concept, Choosing Data Structures, clean educational graphics]
Use a tuple for a fixed ordered group. [Visual: animated programming concept, Choosing Data Structures, clean educational graphics]
Use a set when uniqueness and membership matter. [Visual: animated programming concept, Choosing Data Structures, clean educational graphics]
Use a dictionary when you need to map keys to values. [Visual: animated programming concept, Choosing Data Structures, clean educational graphics]
There is no single best structure for every problem. [Visual: animated programming concept, Choosing Data Structures, clean educational graphics]
Ask: Do I need order? [Visual: animated programming concept, Choosing Data Structures, clean educational graphics]
Do I need unique values? [Visual: animated programming concept, Choosing Data Structures, clean educational graphics]
Do I need key-based lookup? [Visual: animated programming concept, Choosing Data Structures, clean educational graphics]
Do I need to modify the collection? [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Choosing Data Structures]
Challenge: Choose a set for unique tags, a dictionary for user information, a list for ordered tasks, and a tuple for a fixed coordinate. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Collection Challenges
script:
This lesson combines everything from the collections section. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Collection Challenges, modern code editor]
Given a list of scores, calculate the average. [Visual: animated programming concept, Collection Challenges, clean educational graphics]
Given a list with duplicates, create unique values. [Visual: animated programming concept, Collection Challenges, clean educational graphics]
Given a dictionary of users, print selected fields. [Visual: animated programming concept, Collection Challenges, clean educational graphics]
The goal is to choose a data structure based on the problem, not based on what syntax you remember first. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Collection Challenges]
Challenge: Find the average of [60, 80, 100]. Answer: sum(scores) / len(scores) = 80. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Practical Collections Project
script:
Let's combine lists and dictionaries into a small report. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Practical Collections Project, modern code editor]
Each student is represented by a dictionary, and all students are stored in a list. [Visual: animated programming concept, Practical Collections Project, clean educational graphics]
We can loop through the records, print names, and calculate an average. [Visual: animated programming concept, Practical Collections Project, clean educational graphics]
This is similar to how real applications represent collections of records. [Visual: animated programming concept, Practical Collections Project, clean educational graphics]
Keep the data structure readable; clear structure makes later changes easier. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Practical Collections Project]
Challenge: Print only students with score >= 80. Answer: add an if inside the loop. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Revision: Collections
script:
Collections are how Python programs handle groups of data. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Revision: Collections, modern code editor]
Lists are ordered and mutable. [Visual: animated programming concept, Revision: Collections, clean educational graphics]
Tuples are ordered and immutable. [Visual: animated programming concept, Revision: Collections, clean educational graphics]
Sets contain unique values. [Visual: animated programming concept, Revision: Collections, clean educational graphics]
Dictionaries map keys to values. [Visual: animated programming concept, Revision: Collections, clean educational graphics]
You should know how to index, slice, loop, modify, and choose between these structures. [Visual: animated programming concept, Revision: Collections, clean educational graphics]
Also review comprehensions as a concise tool, not a replacement for every loop. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Revision: Collections]
Challenge: Which structure is best for unique tags? Answer: a set is a natural choice. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

script:
Exam time. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Exam #3: Collections, modern code editor]
Solve before revealing the answer. [Visual: animated programming concept, Exam #3: Collections, clean educational graphics]
One: get the last item of a list. [Visual: animated programming concept, Exam #3: Collections, clean educational graphics]

The important part is explaining your choice, not only producing code. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Exam #3: Collections]
