[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Functions
script:
Functions package reusable behavior. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Functions, modern code editor]
Instead of copying the same code, define it once and call it whenever needed. [Visual: animated programming concept, Functions, clean educational graphics]
A function can receive inputs and return an output. [Visual: animated programming concept, Functions, clean educational graphics]
This makes programs easier to test, read, and change. [Visual: animated programming concept, Functions, clean educational graphics]
Start with a function that prints a message, then gradually add parameters and return values. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Functions]
Challenge: Create a function called welcome that prints 'Welcome to Python'. Answer: define it with def and call welcome(). [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Creating Functions
script:
A function definition starts with def, a name, parentheses, and a colon. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Creating Functions, modern code editor]
The indented body contains the instructions. [Visual: animated programming concept, Creating Functions, clean educational graphics]
Parameters are names that receive values when the function is called. [Visual: animated programming concept, Creating Functions, clean educational graphics]
Use descriptive function names that describe an action. [Visual: animated programming concept, Creating Functions, clean educational graphics]
Functions should usually do one clear job; this makes them easier to reuse. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Creating Functions]
Challenge: Create add(a, b) that prints their sum. Answer: def add(a,b): print(a+b). [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Parameters
script:
Parameters let one function work with different data. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Parameters, modern code editor]
When you call the function, the values you provide are arguments. [Visual: animated programming concept, Parameters, clean educational graphics]
You can have multiple parameters, and the order matters for positional arguments. [Visual: animated programming concept, Parameters, clean educational graphics]
Later we will learn keyword arguments and defaults. [Visual: animated programming concept, Parameters, clean educational graphics]
Think of parameters as inputs to a small reusable machine. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Parameters]
Challenge: Make a function that accepts price and quantity. Answer: def total(price, quantity): and use price * quantity. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: return
script:
return sends a value back to the code that called the function. [Visual: clean programming course title card, return, modern code editor]
This is different from print: print displays something, while return gives the value back so it can be stored or used in another expression. [Visual: animated programming concept, return, clean educational graphics]
Once return runs, the function ends. [Visual: animated programming concept, return, clean educational graphics]
Prefer return when a function calculates a result that another part of the program should control. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating return]
Challenge: Write square(n) that returns n*n. Answer: def square(n): return n*n. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Default Arguments
script:
A default argument is used when the caller does not provide that parameter. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Default Arguments, modern code editor]
This is useful for optional settings. [Visual: animated programming concept, Default Arguments, clean educational graphics]
Required parameters normally come before default parameters. [Visual: animated programming concept, Default Arguments, clean educational graphics]
Default values are evaluated when the function definition is created, so avoid mutable objects such as [] as defaults when you are not intentionally using that behavior. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Default Arguments]
Challenge: Create power(base, exponent=2). Answer: return base ** exponent. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Multiple Arguments
script:
Functions can accept several arguments. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Multiple Arguments, modern code editor]
Positional arguments match parameters by order. [Visual: animated programming concept, Multiple Arguments, clean educational graphics]
Keyword arguments match by parameter name, which can improve readability. [Visual: animated programming concept, Multiple Arguments, clean educational graphics]
You can mix positional arguments before keyword arguments. [Visual: animated programming concept, Multiple Arguments, clean educational graphics]
When a function has many options, keyword arguments make calls easier to understand and reduce mistakes. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Multiple Arguments]
Challenge: Call the function using age=17 and city='Cairo' as keywords. Answer: profile('John', age=17, city='Cairo'). [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Scope
script:
Scope determines where a variable name can be accessed. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Scope, modern code editor]
A variable created inside a function is local to that function. [Visual: animated programming concept, Scope, clean educational graphics]
A variable created outside is global to the module. [Visual: animated programming concept, Scope, clean educational graphics]
Prefer passing values into functions and returning results instead of relying heavily on globals. [Visual: animated programming concept, Scope, clean educational graphics]
This keeps functions predictable. [Visual: animated programming concept, Scope, clean educational graphics]
If Python cannot find a name in the local scope, it searches enclosing, global, and built-in scopes according to its name-resolution rules. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Scope]
Challenge: Why do the two print calls show different x values? Answer: the function creates a local x that shadows the global x. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: *args
script:
*args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple. [Visual: clean programming course title card, *args, modern code editor]
This is useful when you do not know how many values the caller will provide. [Visual: animated programming concept, *args, clean educational graphics]
Inside the function, args behaves like a tuple, so you can loop over it. [Visual: animated programming concept, *args, clean educational graphics]
The star is also used when unpacking an iterable into separate arguments. [Visual: animated programming concept, *args, clean educational graphics]
Focus first on the function parameter behavior. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating *args]
Challenge: Write average(*numbers). Answer: return sum(numbers) / len(numbers). [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: **kwargs
script:
**kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dictionary. [Visual: clean programming course title card, **kwargs, modern code editor]
It is useful for flexible configuration and functions that accept optional named settings. [Visual: animated programming concept, **kwargs, clean educational graphics]
Inside the function, kwargs is a dictionary, so you can inspect keys and values. [Visual: animated programming concept, **kwargs, clean educational graphics]
The double-star is also used to unpack a dictionary into keyword arguments when calling a function. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating **kwargs]
Challenge: Create a function that prints all settings passed as keywords. Answer: loop through kwargs.items(). [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: lambda
script:
A lambda is a small anonymous function written as lambda parameters: expression. [Visual: clean programming course title card, lambda, modern code editor]
It is useful for short transformations or as a function argument. [Visual: animated programming concept, lambda, clean educational graphics]
Do not force complex logic into a lambda; a normal def is clearer. [Visual: animated programming concept, lambda, clean educational graphics]
Lambdas become especially useful with tools such as sorted, map, and filter, which we will revisit later. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating lambda]
Challenge: Create a lambda that returns the square of x. Answer: lambda x: x*x. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Modules
script:
A module is a Python file that contains reusable code. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Modules, modern code editor]
As projects grow, putting everything in one file becomes difficult to manage. [Visual: animated programming concept, Modules, clean educational graphics]
You can create a helper.py file and import functions from it. [Visual: animated programming concept, Modules, clean educational graphics]
This is the beginning of organizing real applications into multiple files. [Visual: animated programming concept, Modules, clean educational graphics]
Keep module names simple and avoid naming your files after standard library modules such as random or json. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Modules]
Challenge: Create a module with a greet function and import it. Answer: from helper import greet. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Importing Modules
script:
Python provides several import styles. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Importing Modules, modern code editor]
import math lets you use math.sqrt. [Visual: animated programming concept, Importing Modules, clean educational graphics]
from math import sqrt imports one name directly. [Visual: animated programming concept, Importing Modules, clean educational graphics]
You can use as to create an alias. [Visual: animated programming concept, Importing Modules, clean educational graphics]
Prefer clear imports and avoid wildcard imports because they make it harder to know where names came from. [Visual: animated programming concept, Importing Modules, clean educational graphics]
Modules provide namespaces that keep related functionality organized. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Importing Modules]
Challenge: Import random and generate a random integer from 1 to 10. Answer: import random; random.randint(1,10). [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Standard Library
script:
Python's standard library gives you many tools without installing third-party packages. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Standard Library, modern code editor]
Examples include math for mathematical functions, random for randomness, datetime for dates and times, pathlib for file paths, json for JSON data, and os for operating-system interactions. [Visual: animated programming concept, Standard Library, clean educational graphics]
The important skill is knowing that you can search the standard library before installing a package. [Visual: animated programming concept, Standard Library, clean educational graphics]
We will use several of these tools in later projects. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Standard Library]
Challenge: Which module is a natural choice for JSON? Answer: the json module. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Useful Utility
script:
Let's create a small utility module to see why organization matters. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Useful Utility, modern code editor]
Put helper functions in one file and import them into a main program. [Visual: animated programming concept, Useful Utility, clean educational graphics]
A utility function should have a clear input and output and avoid unnecessary global state. [Visual: animated programming concept, Useful Utility, clean educational graphics]
This pattern scales from tiny scripts to larger projects. [Visual: animated programming concept, Useful Utility, clean educational graphics]
The lesson is not the specific function; it is the habit of separating reusable logic from the program that uses it. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Useful Utility]
Challenge: Add is_positive(n). Answer: return n > 0. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Revision + Exam #4
script:
Before files and errors, review function fundamentals. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Revision + Exam #4, modern code editor]
You should know how to define and call functions, use parameters, return values, defaults, keyword arguments, *args, **kwargs, lambdas, scope, and modules. [Visual: animated programming concept, Revision + Exam #4, clean educational graphics]
Exam question: write a function that accepts any number of scores and returns their average. [Visual: animated programming concept, Revision + Exam #4, clean educational graphics]
Then create a helper module and import that function. [Visual: animated programming concept, Revision + Exam #4, clean educational graphics]
The point is reusable design. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Revision + Exam #4]
Answers: use *scores for flexible positional arguments, sum and len for the average, and return the result. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Reading Files
script:
Programs often need to read data from files. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Reading Files, modern code editor]
Python's open function can open a file, and the with statement automatically closes it afterward. [Visual: animated programming concept, Reading Files, clean educational graphics]
Use mode 'r' for reading. [Visual: animated programming concept, Reading Files, clean educational graphics]
read gets the entire contents, readline reads one line, and readlines returns lines. [Visual: animated programming concept, Reading Files, clean educational graphics]
File paths can be tricky, so later pathlib will make them easier. [Visual: animated programming concept, Reading Files, clean educational graphics]
Always handle missing files appropriately in real applications. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Reading Files]
Challenge: Read a file line by line. Answer: for line in file: print(line.strip()). [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Writing Files
script:
To write a file, open it with mode 'w'. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Writing Files, modern code editor]
This creates the file if it does not exist and replaces its existing contents. [Visual: animated programming concept, Writing Files, clean educational graphics]
Mode 'a' appends instead. [Visual: animated programming concept, Writing Files, clean educational graphics]
The with statement still handles closing the file. [Visual: animated programming concept, Writing Files, clean educational graphics]
Be careful with 'w' because it can erase data. [Visual: animated programming concept, Writing Files, clean educational graphics]
In real projects, decide deliberately whether you want replace or append behavior. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Writing Files]
Challenge: Append a new line without deleting the old text. Answer: use mode 'a'. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: CSV
script:
CSV means comma-separated values and is common for tables. [Visual: clean programming course title card, CSV, modern code editor]
Python's csv module handles quoting and separators more safely than manually splitting every line. [Visual: animated programming concept, CSV, clean educational graphics]
Use csv.reader for rows and csv.DictReader when the first row contains column names. [Visual: animated programming concept, CSV, clean educational graphics]
For output, csv.writer or DictWriter can create structured files. [Visual: animated programming concept, CSV, clean educational graphics]
CSV is useful for small datasets and exports. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating CSV]
Challenge: Why prefer csv over simple split(',')? Answer: CSV can contain quoted commas and other formatting rules. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Exceptions
script:
Programs encounter errors: invalid input, missing files, network problems, and many other situations. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Exceptions, modern code editor]
Python represents many runtime problems as exceptions. [Visual: animated programming concept, Exceptions, clean educational graphics]
Instead of letting the program crash immediately, you can catch specific exceptions and respond appropriately. [Visual: animated programming concept, Exceptions, clean educational graphics]
Do not catch every possible error blindly; catching a specific exception makes debugging and behavior clearer. [Visual: animated programming concept, Exceptions, clean educational graphics]
Exceptions are part of normal robust program design. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Exceptions]
Challenge: What exception does int('abc') raise? Answer: ValueError. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: try/except
script:
Use try for code that may raise an expected exception and except to handle it. [Visual: clean programming course title card, try/except, modern code editor]
Catch the narrowest useful exception. [Visual: animated programming concept, try/except, clean educational graphics]
For example, int conversion can raise ValueError. [Visual: animated programming concept, try/except, clean educational graphics]
After handling the error, your program can ask again or choose a fallback. [Visual: animated programming concept, try/except, clean educational graphics]
Error handling should not hide bugs; it should make expected failure modes manageable. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating try/except]
Challenge: Handle a missing file. Answer: catch FileNotFoundError around the open call. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: finally
script:
finally runs whether an exception happened or not. [Visual: clean programming course title card, finally, modern code editor]
It is useful for cleanup operations that must happen in both success and failure cases. [Visual: animated programming concept, finally, clean educational graphics]
In modern Python, with statements often handle resource cleanup more elegantly for files and similar resources. [Visual: animated programming concept, finally, clean educational graphics]
Still, understanding finally helps you read and maintain code that needs guaranteed cleanup. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating finally]
Challenge: Explain why 'Finished' prints even after an error. Answer: finally runs after try/except regardless of whether an exception occurred. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Debugging
script:
Debugging means finding why actual behavior differs from expected behavior. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Debugging, modern code editor]
Start by reproducing the problem. [Visual: animated programming concept, Debugging, clean educational graphics]
Read the traceback from the bottom upward to find the exception and location. [Visual: animated programming concept, Debugging, clean educational graphics]
Print important values before the failing line. [Visual: animated programming concept, Debugging, clean educational graphics]
Reduce the problem to the smallest example you can. [Visual: animated programming concept, Debugging, clean educational graphics]
Fix one thing at a time and test again. [Visual: animated programming concept, Debugging, clean educational graphics]
A debugger in VS Code can also pause execution and inspect variables, but the reasoning process is more important than the tool. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Debugging]
Challenge: If a variable is unexpectedly 0, where should you look? Answer: trace where it was created or changed and print its value at key points. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: OOP
script:
Object-oriented programming groups data and behavior into objects. [Visual: clean programming course title card, OOP, modern code editor]
A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance created from that blueprint. [Visual: animated programming concept, OOP, clean educational graphics]
For example, a Player class might contain a name and score and methods that change the score. [Visual: animated programming concept, OOP, clean educational graphics]
OOP is one tool, not a requirement for every small script. [Visual: animated programming concept, OOP, clean educational graphics]
Learn it because many real Python libraries use classes, and larger programs often benefit from organizing related behavior together. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating OOP]
Challenge: Create an empty Book class and instantiate it. Answer: class Book: pass; book = Book(). [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Classes
script:
A class can define methods and create attributes for each object. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Classes, modern code editor]
The special __init__ method runs when an object is created and can store initial data. [Visual: animated programming concept, Classes, clean educational graphics]
Methods receive self as their first parameter, which refers to the current object. [Visual: animated programming concept, Classes, clean educational graphics]
This lets each instance keep its own state. [Visual: animated programming concept, Classes, clean educational graphics]
Keep the first examples small so the relationship between class, object, and self is clear. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Classes]
Challenge: Create a Car class with a brand attribute. Answer: set self.brand in __init__. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Objects
script:
Objects created from the same class share the class definition but hold their own instance data. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Objects, modern code editor]
If you create two Player objects with different names, changing one player's name does not change the other. [Visual: animated programming concept, Objects, clean educational graphics]
This is the core benefit of instances: one blueprint can represent many independent entities. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Objects]
Challenge: Create two Student objects with different names. Answer: call the class twice with different arguments. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: __init__
script:
__init__ is called automatically when you create an object. [Visual: clean programming course title card, __init__, modern code editor]
It receives the arguments passed to the class and assigns initial attributes. [Visual: animated programming concept, __init__, clean educational graphics]
The first parameter is self. [Visual: animated programming concept, __init__, clean educational graphics]
The double underscores are part of the special method name. [Visual: animated programming concept, __init__, clean educational graphics]
You usually do not call __init__ directly. [Visual: animated programming concept, __init__, clean educational graphics]
Think of it as the setup step for a new object. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating __init__]
Challenge: Add a currency attribute with default 'USD'. Answer: add currency='USD' to __init__ and assign self.currency. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Instance Methods
script:
Instance methods are functions defined inside a class that operate on an object's state. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Instance Methods, modern code editor]
They take self first, then any additional arguments. [Visual: animated programming concept, Instance Methods, clean educational graphics]
Calling account.deposit(50) automatically passes account as self. [Visual: animated programming concept, Instance Methods, clean educational graphics]
Methods keep related behavior close to the data they manipulate. [Visual: animated programming concept, Instance Methods, clean educational graphics]
This makes object-oriented code easier to reason about when the objects represent real entities. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Instance Methods]
Challenge: Add withdraw(amount) that subtracts from balance. Answer: self.balance -= amount, with appropriate validation in real code. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Inheritance
script:
Inheritance lets one class derive from another. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Inheritance, modern code editor]
The child class gets attributes and methods from the parent and can add or override behavior. [Visual: animated programming concept, Inheritance, clean educational graphics]
Use inheritance when there is a genuine 'is a' relationship. [Visual: animated programming concept, Inheritance, clean educational graphics]
Do not use it just to avoid a few lines of code; composition is often better for many designs. [Visual: animated programming concept, Inheritance, clean educational graphics]
Python uses class Child(Parent) syntax. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Inheritance]
Challenge: Create Cat(Animal) with speak printing 'Meow'. Answer: define class Cat(Animal) and override speak. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Encapsulation
script:
Encapsulation means keeping an object's internal details behind a clear interface. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Encapsulation, modern code editor]
Python does not enforce private fields in the same way some languages do, but naming conventions such as a leading underscore communicate that an attribute is internal. [Visual: animated programming concept, Encapsulation, clean educational graphics]
Double underscores trigger name mangling. [Visual: animated programming concept, Encapsulation, clean educational graphics]
The bigger lesson is design: expose methods that express what the object should do instead of making every caller manipulate internal state directly. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Encapsulation]
Challenge: Why use a method instead of changing _value everywhere? Answer: it keeps control of how the state changes. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

This is a learning project, not real financial software. [Visual: animated programming concept, OOP Project + Revision, clean educational graphics]

title: Iterators
script:
An iterable is something you can loop over. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Iterators, modern code editor]
An iterator is an object that produces values one at a time using next. [Visual: animated programming concept, Iterators, clean educational graphics]
Calling iter on a list gives an iterator. [Visual: animated programming concept, Iterators, clean educational graphics]
Each next call advances it, and when values are exhausted Python raises StopIteration. [Visual: animated programming concept, Iterators, clean educational graphics]
A for loop uses this protocol for you. [Visual: animated programming concept, Iterators, clean educational graphics]
Understanding iterators helps explain how Python handles loops and lazy data. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Iterators]
Challenge: What happens after the third next call? Answer: the next call raises StopIteration. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Generators
script:
A generator function uses yield instead of return to produce values one at a time. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Generators, modern code editor]
Each time next is called, execution resumes where it left off. [Visual: animated programming concept, Generators, clean educational graphics]
Generators are useful when a sequence is large or expensive to create because values do not all need to exist in memory at once. [Visual: animated programming concept, Generators, clean educational graphics]
A for loop can consume a generator naturally. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Generators]
Challenge: Why can generators save memory? Answer: they produce values lazily instead of storing the entire sequence at once. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Decorators
script:
A decorator is a function that takes another function and returns a modified or wrapped function. [Visual: clean programming course title card, Decorators, modern code editor]
The @syntax is a convenient way to apply one. [Visual: animated programming concept, Decorators, clean educational graphics]
Decorators are common in web frameworks, logging, authorization, caching, and timing. [Visual: animated programming concept, Decorators, clean educational graphics]
Start by understanding the idea: a function can receive another function as data because functions are first-class objects in Python. [Visual: Python code editor and terminal output illustrating Decorators]
Challenge: What does @log_call do? Answer: it replaces hello with the wrapper returned by log_call. [Visual: coding challenge card with Python editor, pause before answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: map
script:
map() applies a function to every item in an iterable and returns a lazy map object. [Visual: Python map function with a list and transformed output]
It is useful when the same transformation should be applied to many values. [Visual: clean Python editor showing map]
Challenge: convert numeric strings into integers. Answer: use map(int, values). [Visual: coding challenge card with answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: filter
script:
filter() keeps only items for which a function returns True. [Visual: Python filter function with values entering and matching values leaving]
It returns a lazy filter object that you can convert to a list. [Visual: clean Python editor showing filter]
Challenge: keep only even numbers. Answer: filter(lambda n: n % 2 == 0, numbers). [Visual: coding challenge card with answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: zip
script:
zip() combines items from multiple iterables by position. [Visual: two Python lists being zipped together]
It is useful for processing related values side by side, and it stops when the shortest iterable ends. [Visual: clean Python editor showing zip]
Challenge: pair names with scores. Answer: loop over zip(names, scores). [Visual: coding challenge card with answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: enumerate
script:
enumerate() gives you both an index and a value while looping. [Visual: Python enumerate loop showing index and value]
It is cleaner than manually maintaining a counter, and start= lets you choose the first index. [Visual: clean Python editor showing enumerate]
Challenge: number items starting at one. Answer: enumerate(items, start=1). [Visual: coding challenge card with answer reveal]
[Visual: on-screen code card showing the lesson's Python example clearly, highlighted lines, terminal result]

title: Advanced Comprehensions
script:
Comprehensions can include conditions and nested loops, but readability comes first. [Visual: Python list comprehension building a filtered list]
Use a simple comprehension when the transformation is obvious; otherwise a normal loop may be clearer. [Visual: comprehension versus loop comparison]
Challenge: squares of even numbers from one to ten. Answer: [n*n for n in range(1, 11) if n % 2 == 0]. [Visual: coding challenge card with answer reveal]

script:

The goal is a project that is easy to change, not a project with unnecessary files. [Visual: clean project architecture]
